newsitem.title: USA: IPO VIEW-Once-dull REITs attract Wall St's eye.
newsitem.headline: IPO VIEW-Once-dull REITs attract Wall St's eye.

text.p: Real estate investment trusts (REITs), once seen as dull investments with sluggish growth prospects, have been showing new spark by raising heaps of cash in the risk-averse IPO market.
Smelling profits, real estate moguls Mort Zuckerman, Samuel Zell, and Australia's Frank Lowy are all planning IPOs to cash in on Wall Street's new-found admiration for REITs.
REITs manage real estate portfolios such as shopping centers, office buildings, or hotels and pay high dividends, which can offer a cushion in a market downturn.

For the past year, REIT returns including dividends beat the Standard & Poor's 500 Index with a 29.3 percent gain compared to the S&P's 25.13 percent, according to NAREIT, a Washington-based industry organization.
"REIT IPOs have been doing a little better than expected. They are actually getting small pops, which is unusual," said John Fitzgibbon, editor of the IPO Aftermarket.

Two features boosting the star status of REITs in today's market climate is their liquidity and high payout ratios. To keep their special federal tax status, they pay out 95 percent of their taxable income to shareholders.

Four REITs have gone public in 1997, raising $674.7 million. Stock offerings of already-public REITs are near chart-topping levels, raising $9.96 billion so far in 1997, well on their way to beating 1996's record $11.20 billion.

The four REIT stocks that went public this year gained on average 9.2 percent (excluding dividends) based on their Friday closing prices, better than their IPO counterparts. According to Fitzgibbon, 1997's IPOs have posted an average gain of eight percent so far this year.

"The REITs have greatly improved their liquidity over the last three years," said Prudential senior real estate analyst Louis Taylor. "They still are not quite as liquid as utilities, but they have the highest absolute yield."

Taylor said with utilities providing relatively slim growth, many investors are using REITs now for high income investments free from the queasiness inspired by Wall Street's daily rollercoaster rides.
And with massive day-to-day fluctuations growing more common in the U.S. stock market, even brave investors are seeking safe havens to park pockets of their portfolio.

Zuckerman's Boston Properties Inc has filed for a $737.5 million IPO, the biggest IPO yet this year and just shy of the top-grossing REIT IPO, the $750 million market debut of Rockefeller Center Properties Inc in September 1985.
Zell's Equity Office Properties Trust has filed for a $300 million IPO of 15 million shares to sell for $20 each.
Next week, a mall REIT run by Lowy, the third richest man in Australia, plans a $300 million IPO of 18 million shares to sell for between $16 and $17.50 each.

The Lowy REIT is called Westfield America and is based in Los Angeles. Analysts, who did not expect strong premiums on the Westfield REIT in the first place, said its debut could be hurt by a critical Wall Street Journal report published Friday.
The report said many REIT experts do not like Westfield's outside advisory structure. Under that arrangement, a separate outside adviser with different ownership will manage the company.
Analysts say, however, they do expect strong Wall Street interest in the Zuckerman and Zell offerings.

"The Class of 1997" IPOs so far this year had posted an average loss of three percent through the end of April before last week's surge in small caps lifted them to an average gain of about eight percent.
But REITs and REIT IPOs have turned in mixed performances against the Standard & Poor's 500 over other time spans.

For 1997 through April 30, REITs have lost two percent compared to the S&P's gain of 8.8 percent, according to NAREIT. They hold up better long term, with a gain of 15.8 percent compared to they S&P's 17 percent over five years.
The four REIT IPOs that have gone public this year are Kilroy Realty Corp, Golf Trust of America, Cornerstone Realty Income Trust Inc and Cornerstone Properties.
Last week, nine initial public offerings raised $577 million, according to MCM Corporate Watch.
((-- Wall Street Desk 212 859-1881))
